opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly I think the line between the two has gotten a lot blurrier than people expect.

The way I tend to think about it is that generation and editing are really the same underlying capability, just with different amounts of conditioning. In pure generation, you're starting from a text prompt and the model has a lot of freedom: it's sampling from a huge space of plausible images that match the description. In editing, you're giving the model an image as part of the input, and now the task is much more constrained. You want it to change specific things while preserving everything else: the identity of a person, the lighting, the composition, the little details that make that image *that* image.

And that preservation part is actually where a lot of the difficulty lives. It's relatively easy to get a model to produce something that looks good. It's much harder to get it to make a precise, targeted change and leave the rest untouched. Older approaches often needed masks or specialized pipelines for that. With a natively multimodal model like Gemini, the image and the text live in the same context, so the model can reason about what you're asking. It understands that "make it nighttime" means changing the lighting and sky, but not turning the person into someone else.

The other thing I'd point out is that because it's conversational, editing becomes iterative. You're not doing one shot and starting over. You can say "now move the lamp to the left," then "actually make the jacket blue," and the model carries that context forward. So in a sense, editing turns into a dialogue with the image, and generation is just the first turn of that dialogue.

So I don't really see them as separate tasks anymore. It's more of a spectrum of how much you're asking the model to keep versus how much you're asking it to imagine.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes generation as starting from a text prompt and editing as taking an image as part of the input.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, and honestly I think the distinction is a little fuzzier than people assume. From the model's perspective, generation and editing are kind of the same task. In both cases you're conditioning on some input and producing an image. The difference is just what's in the context. For pure generation, the conditioning is text only. For editing, the conditioning includes one or more images plus text, and the model is expected to preserve most of what's in those images while changing some subset of it.

So technically they live on a spectrum. If I hand the model a photo and say "make this a watercolor painting," is that an edit or a generation? Structurally it's an edit, because the composition and layout are preserved. Stylistically it's close to a generation, because almost every pixel changes. And then on the other end you have something like "remove the person in the background," where you want ninety-five percent of the image to be bit-for-bit identical and only a small region to be reimagined.

Where I think the distinction really matters is in what the model has to be good at. Generation is mostly about priors. Does the model know what things look like, can it compose a scene, does it follow the prompt. Editing adds this whole other requirement, which is faithfulness to the input. You need to understand what's in the image, what the user is pointing at, often implicitly, and what should stay fixed. That's much closer to an understanding problem than a synthesis problem. And that's actually why I think it's so natural to do this in a model like Gemini that's natively multimodal. The same representation that lets the model answer questions about an image is what lets it reason about which parts of the image to touch. You're not bolting an editor onto a generator. The editing capability kind of falls out of having understanding and generation in one place.

The other thing I'd say is that from a user's point of view, editing is often the more useful mode. Most people don't actually start from nothing. They have a photo, a product shot, a sketch, and they want to iterate on it. So a lot of what we think about is the conversational loop, where you generate something, then edit it, then edit the edit, and the model has to keep track of all of that in context. At that point the generation-versus-editing split really dissolves. It's just a conversation that happens to include pixels.

r001.rationale: It says generation is conditioned on text only, while editing is conditioned on one or more images plus text, identifying the distinction as a difference in input modalities.

astra-6.text:
I think of them as closely related tasks. With generation, you’re usually starting from a text prompt and asking the model to create an image. With editing, you’re giving it an existing image and asking for a particular change. That image becomes part of the specification: it tells the model what’s already there and, implicitly, what should stay the same.

So if I ask you to change someone’s shirt from blue to red, the challenge isn’t just producing a plausible person in a red shirt. It’s preserving that person, their pose, the background, and all the details I didn’t ask you to change. You need both an understanding of the instruction and a very precise relationship to the input image.

In a multimodal model like Gemini, you can think of both as generating an image conditioned on context. But editing places a much stronger constraint on fidelity to that context. And conversationally, the boundary gets blurry: you might generate something, then refine it over several turns, with each result becoming the starting point for the next edit.

r001.rationale: The response says generation starts from a text prompt, while editing takes an existing image as input, clearly identifying the input-modality distinction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of generation and editing as closely related problems. With generation, you’re describing an image you want the model to create. With editing, you’re also giving it an existing image, and that image provides a lot of constraints: here’s the person, here’s the scene, here’s the composition. Then you’re asking it to change something while preserving the things you care about.

So the challenge isn’t just producing a plausible image. It’s understanding what should change and what should stay the same. If I ask you to change someone’s shirt, I generally expect their face, their pose, and the background to remain consistent, even if I don’t explicitly say that.

In a multimodal model like Gemini, those tasks can live within the same interaction. You can generate something, talk about it, and refine it over multiple turns. From the user’s perspective, the boundary becomes less important than whether the model understands their intent and makes the right changes.

r001.rationale: The response says generation starts from a description, while editing also uses an existing image, but it does not identify the distinction as a difference in the input modalities a model accepts.
